# 1. Introduction

Handwriting is individual enough that examiners routinely use it to judge who wrote a document. @srihari2002 analysed samples from 1,500 writers and reported that a statistical model could tell, with about 96% confidence, whether two handwriting samples came from the same writer. Deep learning has since been applied to the same problem. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), whose use for digit recognition was established by @lecun1998, have been used to identify writers from images of their handwriting [@fiel2015; @xing2016]. Deciding whether two samples share an author can instead be treated as a similarity-learning problem. @bromley1993 introduced the "Siamese" architecture for signature verification, in which two inputs pass through the same network with shared weights and are compared in the output space. This report seeks to use two neural network models (CNN and Siamese) for writer identification of simulated digit images.

```{r}
# Draw one image from its row number
draw_image <- function(i){
  m <- data$images[i, , , 1]
  image(t(m[28:1, ]), col = gray.colors(256, start = 1, end = 0),
        axes = FALSE, asp = 1)
}

# All 20 writers for one digit (session and replicate fixed)
plot_writers <- function(d, s = 1, r = 1){
  op <- par(mfrow = c(4, 5), mar = c(0.3, 0.3, 1.5, 0.3), oma = c(0, 0, 2.5, 0))
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (p in 1:20){
    i <- which(metadata$person_id == p & metadata$digit == d &
                 metadata$session == s & metadata$replicate == r)
    draw_image(i)
    title(paste("Writer", p), cex.main = 0.9)
  }
  mtext(paste0("Digit ", d, " (session ", s, ", replicate ", r, ")"),
        outer = TRUE, font = 2)
}

# Random sample of writers across sessions (replicate fixed)
plot_sessions_sample <- function(d, n_people = 10, r = 1, seed = 1){
  set.seed(seed)
  people <- sort(sample(1:20, n_people))
  op <- par(mfrow = c(n_people, 5), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 1.2, 0.2),
            oma = c(0, 5, 2.5, 0), xpd = NA)
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (p in people){
    for (s in 1:5){
      i <- which(metadata$person_id == p & metadata$digit == d &
                   metadata$session == s & metadata$replicate == r)
      draw_image(i)
      if (p == people[1]) title(paste("Session", s), cex.main = 0.9)
      if (s == 1) mtext(paste("Writer", p), side = 2, line = 0.5, las = 1, cex = 0.7)
    }
  }
  mtext(paste0("Digit ", d, " across sessions (replicate ", r, ")"),
        outer = TRUE, font = 2)
}

# Same writers across replicates (session fixed)
plot_replicates <- function(d, s = 1, n_people = 10,
                            reps = c(1, 11, 21, 31, 41), seed = 1){
  set.seed(seed)
  people <- sort(sample(1:20, n_people))
  op <- par(mfrow = c(n_people, length(reps)), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 1.2, 0.2),
            oma = c(0, 5, 2.5, 0), xpd = NA)
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (p in people){
    for (r in reps){
      i <- which(metadata$person_id == p & metadata$digit == d &
                   metadata$session == s & metadata$replicate == r)
      draw_image(i)
      if (p == people[1]) title(paste("Replicate", r), cex.main = 0.9)
      if (r == reps[1]) mtext(paste("Writer", p), side = 2, line = 0.5, las = 1, cex = 0.7)
    }
  }
  mtext(paste0("Digit ", d, " across replicates (session ", s, ")"),
        outer = TRUE, font = 2)
}
```

## 2.1 Data Overview

The data consisted of 25,000 greyscale images of 28 x 28 pixels, showing the digits 0 to 4. Each of the 20 writers wrote each digit 50 times (replicate) in each of the 5 sessions, giving a total of 1,250 images per writer. The original pixel values \[0,255\], were scaled to \[0, 1\] before fitting the neural network models, because scaling the pixel values creates a stable foundation for gradient optimisation @afzali2026. The metadata contains the image ID, writer ID, digit, session number and replicate number. To explore the sources of variability in the data, four analyses were carried out including variation between writers, variation across sessions for a subset of writers, variation within sessions (across replicates) for a subset of writers, and a quantitative comparison of the three using pixel distances.

## 2.2 Variation between writers

To examine variation between writers, each digit was plotted for all 20 writers, with session and replicate fixed at 1. This produced five plots, one per digit. @williams2019 states that no two people's handwriting can ever be the same: they may have a similar style but they will differ in the characteristics of their handwriting. Variability that distinguishes one person's handwriting from another's was therefore assessed using characteristics such as size, shape and slant. @fig-writers shows clear differences in handwriting style between the 20 writers.

```{r}
#| label: fig-writers
#| fig-cap: "[Digits 0 (a) and 1 (b) for all 20 writers, with session 1 and replicate 1 fixed.]"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
plot_writers(c(0, 1))
```

Variation in shape is most clearly observed in digits 0 and 1 (@fig-writers). For example, although all the 1s have a base, some have a hook at the top (writers 1, 7 and 14), while others have a curved body that resembles the digit 2 (writers 3, 9 and 17). For digit 0, shapes vary from circular to oval. The remaining digits follow a more consistent style, with the primary differences being slant and size. Size also varies whereby some writers (3 and 9) write small and compact digits, while others fill the space with large digits. Slant varies from upright to a rightward slant (writers 18 and 10), while writer 19 slants to the left. These differences in size, shape and slant are features that the models could learn for writer identification, although some digits may reveal more information than others. Digits 0 and 1, which show more shape variation across writers, may provide stronger information for distinguishing between writers than digits 2, 3 and 4, whose shapes are more uniform.

## 2.3 Variation across sessions

To assess whether a person's handwriting changes between sessions, 10 writers were randomly sampled and each digit was plotted across the 5 sessions, with the replicate fixed at 1.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 10
plot_sessions_sample(c(1, 0))
```

```{r}
#| label: save-sessions

for (d in 0:4){
  png(sprintf("results/sessions_digit_%d.png", d), width = 700, height = 1000)
  plot_sessions_sample(d)
  invisible(dev.off())

```

There are visible changes in style between sessions, and these are more noticeable for some digits than others, such as 0 and 1. Although some changes are noticeable, some writers remained consistent in certain characteristics. For example, writer 3 wrote small digits in all sessions and, for digit 1, kept their signature hook in every session, as writer 17 did. Other writers changed their characteristic style, for example, writer 19 slanted the digits slightly to the left in the first session, but the digits became more upright as the sessions progressed. Writer 1's 1s also changed between sessions because some have hooks and the lengths of the strokes differ. This indicates that a writer's handwriting may change between sessions. Although some of these changes are minor, they alter a writer's characteristic style from session 1, so the models may identify some writers less accurately in a new session.

## 2.5 Quantifying the variation

To quantify the variation between writers, across sessions and within sessions, the euclidean distance between two images was computed over all 784 pixels. For a sample of 1,000 draws, the function picked a writer, a digit, two sessions and two replicates and formed three comparisons with the digit matched within a session (comparing replicates), across sessions (the same writer) and between writers. The three distances were compared using a Friedman test @friedman1937, followed by the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests @wilcoxon1945 adjusted with the Holm's method @holm1979. The paired effect size d~z~ was also reported, and defined as the mean paired difference divided by the standard deviation of the differences @lakens2013. Intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals from the 2000 resamples of the draws @efron1979.

```{r}
#| label: task1-distances
#| include: false
# Flatten each 28x28 image into one row of 784 pixel values (scaled 0-1)
x_flat <- matrix(data$images / 255, nrow = dim(data$images)[1])

# Find the row number of one specific image
get_i <- function(p, d, s, r){
  which(metadata$person_id == p & metadata$digit == d &
          metadata$session == s & metadata$replicate == r)
}

# Euclidean distance between two images (given their row numbers)
dist_img <- function(a, b) sqrt(sum((x_flat[a, ] - x_flat[b, ])^2))

set.seed(1)
n <- 1000
results <- data.frame(type = character(), digit = integer(), dist = numeric())

for (k in 1:n){
  p <- sample(1:20, 1)                  # a random writer
  d <- sample(0:4, 1)                   # a random digit
  s <- sample(1:5, 2)                   # two different sessions
  r <- sample(1:50, 2)                  # two different replicates
  q <- sample(setdiff(1:20, p), 1)      # a different writer
  
  a <- get_i(p, d, s[1], r[1])          # the reference image
  
  results[nrow(results) + 1, ] <- list("Within-session", d, dist_img(a, get_i(p, d, s[1], r[2])))
  results[nrow(results) + 1, ] <- list("Across-session", d, dist_img(a, get_i(p, d, s[2], r[2])))
  results[nrow(results) + 1, ] <- list("Between-writer", d, dist_img(a, get_i(q, d, s[1], r[2])))
}

results$type <- factor(results$type,
                       levels = c("Within-session", "Across-session", "Between-writer"))

```

```{r}
#| label: task1-stats
#| include: false
# Helpers used by the inline numbers in the text
f2 <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
fp <- function(p) if (p < 1e-16) "< 1e-16" else paste("=", signif(p, 2))

# rows = draws; the 3 distances of a draw are matched
M <- matrix(results$dist, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE,
            dimnames = list(NULL, c("Within", "Across", "Between")))
dig <- results$digit[seq(1, nrow(results), by = 3)]        # digit of each draw

set.seed(2026)
B <- 2000
boot_q <- function(v, f = mean) unname(quantile(replicate(B, f(sample(v, length(v), replace = TRUE))), c(.025, .975)))

desc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(M), function(nm) {
  v <- M[, nm]; ci <- boot_q(v)
  data.frame(Pair = nm, n = length(v), Mean = mean(v), SD = sd(v), Median = median(v),
             IQR = IQR(v), CI_low = ci[1], CI_high = ci[2])
}))
desc$Pair <- c("Within-session", "Across-session", "Between-writer")  

fr <- friedman.test(M)
kendall_w <- unname(fr$statistic) / (nrow(M) * (ncol(M) - 1))

pw <- do.call(rbind, lapply(list(c("Within", "Across"), c("Within", "Between"), c("Across", "Between")), function(p) {
  d <- M[, p[2]] - M[, p[1]]; ci <- boot_q(d)
  data.frame(Comparison = paste(p[2], "minus", p[1]), Mean_diff = mean(d), CI_low = ci[1], CI_high = ci[2],
             d_z = mean(d) / sd(d),
             p_raw = wilcox.test(M[, p[2]], M[, p[1]], paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE)$p.value)
}))
pw$p_Holm <- p.adjust(pw$p_raw, method = "holm")

ratio_by_digit <- do.call(rbind, lapply(0:4, function(dg) {
  ix <- which(dig == dg); w <- M[ix, "Within"]; a <- M[ix, "Across"]
  bs <- replicate(B, { s <- sample.int(length(ix), replace = TRUE); mean(a[s]) / mean(w[s]) })
  data.frame(Digit = dg, n = length(ix), Within = mean(w), Across = mean(a),
             Between = mean(M[ix, "Between"]),                                
             Ratio = mean(a) / mean(w),
             CI_low = unname(quantile(bs, .025)), CI_high = unname(quantile(bs, .975)))
}))
```

Two images of the same digit by the same writer in the same session were near identical (mean distance = 2.72, SD = 0.50), which indicates that the 50 replicates are near copies of one another. The across session of the same writer has a mean distance of 7.15 and SD = 1.63. The highest variation was recorded between the different writers (mean distance = 8.59, SD = 1.14) (\@tbl_t1_desc, @fig-tl-dist). The three distances differ clearly in the matched draws (Friedman chi-squared = `r f2(unname(fr$statistic), 1)` on `r unname(fr$parameter)` df, p `r fp(fr$p.value)`; Kendall’s W = `r f2(kendall_w)`), and all three Holm-adjusted pairwise tests give p \< 1e-16 (\@tbl-t1-tests).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t1-desc
#| tbl-cap: "Pixel distance between two images of the same digit, by comparison type (1,000 draws), with 95% bootstrap intervals for the mean."
knitr::kable(desc, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, align = "lccccccc",
             col.names = c("Comparison", "Draws", "Mean", "SD", "Median", "IQR",
                           "95% CI low", "95% CI high"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-dist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of pixel distances by comparison type."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
boxplot(M, names = c("Within-session", "Across-session", "Between-writer"),
        ylab = "Pixel distance")
```

With 1,000 draws almost any difference would be significant, so the effect sizes are more informative than the p-values. The across-session minus within-session gap is 4.43 (95% CI 4.33 to 4.53; \$d_z\$ = 2.72), whereas the between-writer minus across-session gap is only 1.44 (95% CI 1.33 to 1.56; \$d_z\$ = 0.77). In practical terms, a change of session moves a writer’s digit about three quarters of the way to where a different writer’s digit sits ((7.15 − 2.72) / (8.59 − 2.72)). A writer is therefore only partly recognisable from the pixels of a single image, and any model has to cope with the same person looking different from one session to the next.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t1-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Paired differences between comparison types: mean difference with 95% bootstrap interval, paired effect size dz, and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank p-values."
tab_tests <- data.frame(
  Comparison = pw$Comparison,
  `Mean difference (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", pw$Mean_diff, pw$CI_low, pw$CI_high),
  dz = round(pw$d_z, 2),
  `Holm-adjusted p` = ifelse(pw$p_Holm < 1e-16, "< 1e-16", signif(pw$p_Holm, 2)),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab_tests, align = "lccc")
```

The ratio of across-session to within-session distance was above 1 for every digit, and its confidence interval never came near 1 (\@fig-t1-ratio, \@tbl-t1-ratio). It was highest for digit 1 (3.40; within-session distance 2.01) and lowest for digit 4 (2.36). Digit 1 is a thin stroke, so a small shift in position or slant changes which pixels are lit, which is a plausible reason for its larger ratio, although this was not tested. \[One sentence on where digit 0 ranks.\] Pixel distance is a crude measure, because a small shift in a digit’s position can inflate the distance between two images of the same shape, so these numbers describe the data and do not by themselves show how well a model can separate writers.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t1-ratio
#| tbl-cap: "Mean pixel distance by digit and comparison type, and the ratio of across-session to within-session distance with a 95% bootstrap interval."
tab_digit <- data.frame(
  Digit = ratio_by_digit$Digit,
  Draws = ratio_by_digit$n,
  `Within-session` = round(ratio_by_digit$Within, 2),
  `Across-session` = round(ratio_by_digit$Across, 2),
  `Between-writer` = round(ratio_by_digit$Between, 2),
  `Across / within (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", ratio_by_digit$Ratio,
                                       ratio_by_digit$CI_low, ratio_by_digit$CI_high),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab_digit, align = "cccccc")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-ratio
#| fig-cap: "Ratio of across-session to within-session distance by digit, with 95% bootstrap intervals. The dashed line marks a ratio of 1."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
plot(ratio_by_digit$Digit, ratio_by_digit$Ratio, pch = 19, xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Digit", ylab = "Across / within distance",
     ylim = range(c(1, ratio_by_digit$CI_low, ratio_by_digit$CI_high)))
axis(1, at = 0:4)
arrows(ratio_by_digit$Digit, ratio_by_digit$CI_low,

abline(h = 1, lty = 2)
```

This has a consequence for how the data are split in the next tasks. A random split would put near-copies of the same image in both the training and the test set, so it would measure memory more than generalisation.

# 3. Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)

Task 2 treats writer identification as a 20-class classification problem: the input is an image and the output is the writer's ID. All 20 writers appear in the training data, so this is identification of known writers, not verification of unknown ones.

**Split.** We split by session: sessions 1 to 3 for training (15 000 images), session 4 for validation and session 5 for testing (5 000 images each). This asks whether a model trained on a person's earlier writing recognises them in a later session, and it stops near-identical replicates (@sec-task1) from straddling the training and test sets. Random splitting of records that share a source is known to give optimistic results: random cross-validation on structured data underestimates predictive error because the dependence between records is ignored [@roberts2017], and @saeb2017 make the same case for subject-wise versus record-wise validation. As a check, we also trained the same model on a random split (15 000 images for training, 5 000 for validation).

**Model.** The CNN has two convolution and max-pooling blocks (32 and then 64 filters of size 3 × 3, following the convolution–pooling design of @lecun1998) with rectified linear activations [@nair2010], a flatten layer, a dense layer of 64 units with 30% dropout, which randomly removes units during training to reduce overfitting [@srivastava2014], and a softmax output of 20 units. We trained with sparse categorical cross-entropy and the Adam optimiser [@kingma2015] for 10 epochs with batches of 128.

**What the measures capture.** Accuracy is the proportion of images assigned to the right writer. In practice it answers: of the pages we receive from known writers in a new session, how many do we attribute to the right person? Chance is 1/20 = 5%, because the 20 writers are equally represented. The confusion matrix shows which writers are mistaken for which, that is, whose handwriting looks alike to the model. Accuracy by digit asks how much writer information a single digit carries, which matters when an examiner only has one kind of character to work with.

**Uncertainty.** The 50 replicates within a writer, digit and session are near copies, so images are not independent and a binomial interval treats the test set as holding more information than it does. We report the exact Clopper–Pearson interval [@clopper1934] for reference, but base our uncertainty on a cluster bootstrap. Whole writer–digit groups (100 in the test session, 20 per digit) are resampled with replacement and the accuracy is recomputed 2000 times [@efron1979; @field2007]. Differences between digits are tested with a Friedman test over writers [@friedman1937], using each writer's accuracy on each digit as the unit.

```{r}
#| label: task2-split
# (Task 2 code as written by the group; data is already loaded above.)
set.seed(1); set_random_seed(1)   # ADDED: makes the training reproducible

x <- data$images / 255
y_person <- data$metadata$person_id - 1L

# Splitting data by session. Session 1-3 for training, session 4 for validation and session 5 for testing

# Picking rows by session
meta <- data$metadata # this is the table with one row per image

train_rows <- which(meta$session %in% 1:3) # row numbers of session 1-3

val_rows <- which(meta$session == 4)
test_rows <- which(meta$session == 5)

# images and labels
x_train <- x[train_rows, , , , drop = FALSE]
y_train <- y_person[train_rows]

x_val <- x[val_rows, , , , drop = FALSE]
y_val <- y_person[val_rows]

x_test <- x[test_rows, , , , drop = FALSE]
y_test <- y_person[test_rows]

# Checking if the split worked
dim(x_train); dim(x_val); dim(x_test)
table(y_train)
```

```{r}
#| label: task2-cnn
# CNN Model building
model <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(28, 28, 1)) |>
  layer_conv_2d(filters = 32, kernel_size = 3, activation = "relu") |> #keeps positive signals only
  layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2) |>       #shrinks the image by half
  layer_conv_2d(filters = 64, kernel_size = 3, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2) |>
  layer_flatten() |>
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.3) |>
  layer_dense(units = 20, activation = "softmax")

# Compiling and training
model |> compile(
  loss = "sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
  optimizer = "adam",
  metrics = "accuracy"
)

history <- model |> fit(
  x_train, y_train,
  epochs = 10,
  batch_size = 128,
  validation_data = list(x_val, y_val),
  verbose = 2   # ADDED: one line per epoch keeps the rendered report tidy
)
```


```{r}
#| label: task2-stats
#| include: false
# ADDED: statistics behind the CNN results
set.seed(2026)
B <- 2000
correct <- pred_class_test == y_test

# Cluster bootstrap: resample whole clusters (e.g. writer x digit groups) with replacement
boot_cluster <- function(correct, cluster, B = 2000) {
  k_c <- tapply(correct, cluster, sum); n_c <- tapply(correct, cluster, length); K <- length(k_c)
  bs <- replicate(B, { i <- sample.int(K, K, replace = TRUE); sum(k_c[i]) / sum(n_c[i]) })
  unname(quantile(bs, c(.025, .975)))
}

n_test <- length(correct); k_test <- sum(correct)
cp_all   <- binom.test(k_test, n_test)$conf.int
boot_all <- boot_cluster(correct, paste(meta_test$person_id, meta_test$digit))

last <- function(v) v[length(v)]
acc_summary <- data.frame(
  Split = c(rep("Session split", 3), rep("Random split", 2)),
  Evaluated_on = c("Training (sessions 1-3), last epoch", "Validation (session 4)", "Test (session 5)",
                   "Training (random), last epoch", "Validation (random)"),
  n = c(length(train_rows), length(val_rows), n_test, length(rand_train), length(rand_val)),
  Accuracy = c(last(history$metrics$accuracy), last(history$metrics$val_accuracy), k_test / n_test,
               last(history_rand$metrics$accuracy), last(history_rand$metrics$val_accuracy)),
  CP_low = c(NA, NA, cp_all[1], NA, NA), CP_high = c(NA, NA, cp_all[2], NA, NA),
  Boot_low = c(NA, NA, boot_all[1], NA, NA), Boot_high = c(NA, NA, boot_all[2], NA, NA))

# Accuracy by digit (clusters = writers within a digit)
digit_stats <- do.call(rbind, lapply(0:4, function(dg) {
  ix <- meta_test$digit == dg; cr <- correct[ix]
  cp <- binom.test(sum(cr), length(cr))$conf.int
  bc <- boot_cluster(cr, meta_test$person_id[ix])
  data.frame(Digit = dg, n = length(cr), Accuracy = mean(cr), CP_low = cp[1], CP_high = cp[2],
             Boot_low = bc[1], Boot_high = bc[2])
}))

# Do digits differ? Friedman test with writers as blocks
cl <- aggregate(correct ~ person + digit,
                data = data.frame(correct = correct, person = meta_test$person_id, digit = meta_test$digit),
                FUN = mean)
acc_mat <- with(cl, tapply(correct, list(person, digit), mean))
fr2 <- friedman.test(acc_mat)
w2 <- unname(fr2$statistic) / (nrow(acc_mat) * (ncol(acc_mat) - 1))

# Accuracy by writer
writer_acc <- data.frame(Writer = as.integer(names(tapply(correct, meta_test$person_id, mean))),
                         Accuracy = as.numeric(tapply(correct, meta_test$person_id, mean)))

# Confusion matrix (rows = true writer, normalised by row)
cm <- table(truth = factor(y_test, levels = 0:19), predicted = factor(pred_class_test, levels = 0:19))
cm_df <- as.data.frame(cm)
cm_df$prop <- cm_df$Freq / ave(cm_df$Freq, cm_df$truth, FUN = sum)
cm_df$truth <- factor(as.integer(as.character(cm_df$truth)) + 1L, levels = 1:20)
cm_df$predicted <- factor(as.integer(as.character(cm_df$predicted)) + 1L, levels = 1:20)
off <- unclass(cm); diag(off) <- 0
top <- head(order(off, decreasing = TRUE), 5)
top_conf <- data.frame(True_writer = row(off)[top] , Predicted_as = col(off)[top], Images = off[top],
                       Share_of_true_writers_images = off[top] / rowSums(unclass(cm))[row(off)[top]])
```

## What Task 2 tells us

The CNN fitted the training sessions almost perfectly (98.7% accuracy after 10 epochs) but identified the writer correctly in only 59.3% of the test images from the unseen session 5 (@tbl-t2-summary). The exact Clopper-Pearson interval is 57.9% to 60.7%, but this treats the 5 000 images as independent, which they are not. The cluster bootstrap, which resamples whole writer-digit groups, gives a much wider interval of 50.3% to 67.8% [@field2007], so the honest statement is that test accuracy is roughly 50% to 68%. Either way it is far above the 5% expected by chance, and far below the training accuracy. The learning curves show where the gap comes from (@fig-t2-curves). Validation accuracy stays between about 46% and 55% from the first epoch, while the validation loss rises from 1.79 to 4.44 as the training loss falls. The network is becoming more confident without becoming more correct on a new session, which is what overfitting looks like. We did not use early stopping here, so the test result is for the model after 10 epochs.

The random split is the contrast that matters. The same network reached 99.5% validation accuracy within ten epochs when the images were shuffled across training and validation. That near-perfect score is not evidence of a better model. It is the leakage that Task 1 predicted, because the validation images have near-copies in the training set (the within-session distance was only 2.72). The gap of about 40 points between the random split (99.5%) and the session-split test (59.3%) shows how much a random split would have overstated performance [@roberts2017; @saeb2017].

Accuracy was similar across digits (55.5% to 69.6%), with digit 3 highest at 69.6%. The cluster-bootstrap intervals for the five digits overlap almost completely (@fig-t2-digit, @tbl-t2-digit), and a Friedman test across digits with writers as blocks gives chi-squared = `r f2(unname(fr2$statistic), 2)` on `r unname(fr2$parameter)` df, p `r fp(fr2$p.value)` (Kendall's W = `r f2(w2)`). The data therefore give little support for saying that some digits identify writers better than others, and the digit 3 result should be treated as a hint at most.

The errors are concentrated in particular writers more than in particular digits (@fig-t2-writer, @fig-t2-confusion). The clearest case is writer 10: 240 of that writer's 250 test images (96%) were assigned to writer 2 (@tbl-t2-confusions). Writer 5 was mistaken for writer 13 in 72% of cases, and writer 13 for writer 5 in 40%, so those two seem to write alike in session 5. The confusion matrix shows that this happens but not why, so we report it as an observation only.

# 4. Siamese network

Task 3 changes the question. Instead of naming the writer, the network judges whether two images were written by the same person, so it can be applied to writers it has never seen (verification instead of identification). We use a Siamese network [@bromley1993]: one encoder turns each image into a 16-number embedding, the same encoder (with shared weights) is applied to both images in a pair, and the model outputs the Euclidean distance between the two embeddings. The encoder has two convolution and max-pooling stages (16 and 32 filters), global average pooling and a dense layer of 16 units.

**Training examples.** Positive pairs show the same writer and negative pairs show different writers, in roughly equal numbers. Both images in a pair show the same digit; otherwise the network could answer "different writer" whenever the digits differ, instead of comparing handwriting. We split by writer before building pairs: writers 1 to 14 for training (8 000 pairs), 15 to 17 for validation (2 000 pairs) and 18 to 20 for testing (2 000 pairs). Pairs are built only inside one part, so no image or writer appears in more than one part. Because the aim is to compare people, testing on unseen writers is the appropriate kind of generalisation.

**Loss.** We use the contrastive loss of @hadsell2006. With $D$ the distance between the two embeddings, $y = 1$ for a same-writer pair and $m = 1$ the margin,

$$L = y\,D^{2} + (1 - y)\,\max(0,\; m - D)^{2}.$$

Same-writer pairs are pulled together, and different-writer pairs are pushed apart only while they are closer than the margin. @hadsell2006 write the same loss with the labels reversed (0 for similar pairs) and a factor of 1/2; we follow the convention of the course slides. We optimised with Adam and early stopping on the validation loss, keeping the best weights.

**Evaluation.** The network outputs a distance, so a decision rule is needed: a pair is called "same writer" if its distance is below a threshold. We chose the threshold on the validation pairs to maximise balanced accuracy, the mean of the true match rate and the true non-match rate [@brodersen2010], and then fixed it for the test pairs. Because one threshold is one operating point, we also report the ROC curve, which plots the true match rate against the false match rate over all thresholds [@fawcett2006], and the area under it (AUC), which is the probability that a randomly chosen same-writer pair has a smaller distance than a randomly chosen different-writer pair [@hanley1982]. Intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals over test pairs [@efron1979] and exact Clopper–Pearson intervals for rates [@clopper1934]. These intervals reflect the sampling of pairs only. The pairs reuse a small set of images from three writers, so we also report results for each test writer separately.

## Pair construction

```{r}
#| label: task3-pairs
set.seed(1); set_random_seed(1)

# 1. Split by WRITER first, so validation/test writers are never seen in training
tr_ids <- which(meta$person_id %in% 1:14)
va_ids <- which(meta$person_id %in% 15:17)
te_ids <- which(meta$person_id %in% 18:20)

# 2. Build pairs INSIDE one part. About half are same-writer (label 1), half
#    different-writer (label 0). Both images in a pair show the SAME digit, so
#    the model has to compare handwriting, not digit shape.
make_pairs <- function(ids, n){
  a <- sample(ids, n, replace = TRUE)
  same <- runif(n) < 0.5
  b <- integer(n)
  for (k in seq_len(n)){
    i <- a[k]
    pool <- ids[meta$digit[ids] == meta$digit[i]]
    pool <- if (same[k]) pool[meta$person_id[pool] == meta$person_id[i]]
            else         pool[meta$person_id[pool] != meta$person_id[i]]
    pool <- setdiff(pool, i)
    b[k] <- pool[sample.int(length(pool), 1)]
  }
  cbind(a, b)
}
make_batch <- function(p) list(
  left  = x[p[, 1], , , , drop = FALSE],
  right = x[p[, 2], , , , drop = FALSE],
  y     = matrix(as.numeric(meta$person_id[p[, 1]] == meta$person_id[p[, 2]]), ncol = 1))

tr_pairs <- make_pairs(tr_ids, 8000)
va_pairs <- make_pairs(va_ids, 2000)
te_pairs <- make_pairs(te_ids, 2000)   # keep the indices so test pairs can be analysed later
train <- make_batch(tr_pairs)
valid <- make_batch(va_pairs)
test  <- make_batch(te_pairs)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t3-pairs
#| tbl-cap: "Composition of the pair sets. Images are never shared between sets because the split is by writer."
pair_sets <- list(Training = tr_pairs, Validation = va_pairs, Test = te_pairs)
comp <- data.frame(
  Set = names(pair_sets),
  Writers = c("1-14", "15-17", "18-20"),
  Pairs = sapply(pair_sets, nrow),
  Same_writer_share = sapply(pair_sets, function(p) mean(meta$person_id[p[, 1]] == meta$person_id[p[, 2]])),
  Same_digit_in_pair = sapply(pair_sets, function(p) all(meta$digit[p[, 1]] == meta$digit[p[, 2]])),
  Distinct_images = sapply(pair_sets, function(p) length(unique(c(p)))))
knitr::kable(comp, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Set", "Writers", "Pairs", "Share same-writer", "Same digit in every pair", "Distinct images"))
```

## Shared encoder and Siamese model

```{r}
#| label: task3-model
# 3. Shared encoder: the same layers (same weights) are used for both images
img_in <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
z <- img_in |>
  layer_conv_2d(16, 3, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_max_pooling_2d(2) |>
  layer_conv_2d(32, 3, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_global_average_pooling_2d() |>
  layer_dense(16)
encoder <- keras_model(img_in, z)

# 4. Siamese model: output = Euclidean distance between the two embeddings
left_in  <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
right_in <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
distance <- list(encoder(left_in), encoder(right_in)) |>
  layer_lambda(f = function(z) {
    op_sqrt(op_sum(op_square(z[[1]] - z[[2]]), axis = 2, keepdims = TRUE) + 1e-7)
  })
siamese <- keras_model(list(left_in, right_in), distance)

# 5. Contrastive loss with margin 1:
#    same pairs (y = 1) are pulled together (loss D^2);
#    different pairs (y = 0) are pushed apart until D >= 1, then left alone.
contrastive_loss <- function(y, d) {
  op_mean(y * op_square(d) + (1 - y) * op_square(op_maximum(1 - d, 0)))
}
siamese |> compile(optimizer = optimizer_adam(1e-3), loss = contrastive_loss)

history_siam <- siamese |> fit(
  list(train$left, train$right), train$y,
  validation_data = list(list(valid$left, valid$right), valid$y),
  epochs = 12, batch_size = 64, verbose = 2,
  # ADDED: stop when validation loss stops improving and keep the best weights
  callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(monitor = "val_loss", patience = 2,
                                           restore_best_weights = TRUE))
)
```

## Threshold, test performance and breakdowns

```{r}
#| label: task3-eval
# 6. Choose the distance threshold on VALIDATION pairs (not on test)
valid_distance <- as.numeric(predict(siamese, list(valid$left, valid$right), verbose = 0))
valid_same <- valid$y[, 1] == 1

# balanced accuracy = average of (true match rate) and (true non-match rate)
bal_acc <- function(d, same, cut){
  pred_same <- d < cut
  (mean(pred_same[same]) + mean(!pred_same[!same])) / 2
}
# AUC = P(a same-writer pair has a smaller distance than a different-writer pair)
auc_dist <- function(d, same){
  r <- rank(d); n1 <- sum(same); n0 <- sum(!same)
  1 - (sum(r[same]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

cuts <- seq(min(valid_distance), max(valid_distance), length.out = 200)
scores <- sapply(cuts, function(cc) bal_acc(valid_distance, valid_same, cc))
threshold <- cuts[which.max(scores)]
c(threshold = threshold, validation_balanced_accuracy = max(scores))

# 7. Evaluate once on TEST pairs (new writers), threshold fixed from validation
test_distance <- as.numeric(predict(siamese, list(test$left, test$right), verbose = 0))
test_same <- test$y[, 1] == 1
pred_same <- test_distance < threshold

c(test_balanced_accuracy = bal_acc(test_distance, test_same, threshold),
  true_match_rate        = mean(pred_same[test_same]),
  true_non_match_rate    = mean(!pred_same[!test_same]))

table(truth = test_same, predicted = pred_same)
```

```{r}
#| label: task3-stats
#| include: false
# ADDED: statistics behind the Siamese results
set.seed(2026)
B <- 1000
n_pairs <- length(test_same)

bal_hat <- bal_acc(test_distance, test_same, threshold)
auc_hat <- auc_dist(test_distance, test_same)
boot_t3 <- t(replicate(B, {
  i <- sample.int(n_pairs, replace = TRUE)
  c(bal = bal_acc(test_distance[i], test_same[i], threshold), auc = auc_dist(test_distance[i], test_same[i]))
}))
tmr_k <- sum(pred_same[test_same]);   tmr_n <- sum(test_same)
tnr_k <- sum(!pred_same[!test_same]); tnr_n <- sum(!test_same)
cp1 <- binom.test(tmr_k, tmr_n)$conf.int; cp0 <- binom.test(tnr_k, tnr_n)$conf.int
t3_metrics <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Balanced accuracy", "True match rate (same writer accepted)",
              "True non-match rate (different writer rejected)", "AUC"),
  Estimate = c(bal_hat, tmr_k / tmr_n, tnr_k / tnr_n, auc_hat),
  CI_low  = c(quantile(boot_t3[, "bal"], .025), cp1[1], cp0[1], quantile(boot_t3[, "auc"], .025)),
  CI_high = c(quantile(boot_t3[, "bal"], .975), cp1[2], cp0[2], quantile(boot_t3[, "auc"], .975)),
  Interval = c("Bootstrap", "Clopper-Pearson", "Clopper-Pearson", "Bootstrap"))

# confusion counts
t3_conf <- data.frame(
  Truth = c("Same writer", "Different writers"),
  Accepted_as_same = c(tmr_k, tnr_n - tnr_k), Rejected_as_different = c(tmr_n - tmr_k, tnr_k))

# ROC curve
roc_cuts <- c(-Inf, sort(unique(test_distance)), Inf)
roc <- data.frame(fpr = sapply(roc_cuts, function(cc) mean(test_distance[!test_same] < cc)),
                  tpr = sapply(roc_cuts, function(cc) mean(test_distance[test_same]  < cc)))

# Same-session versus different-session pairs
same_session <- meta$session[te_pairs[, 1]] == meta$session[te_pairs[, 2]]
cond <- function(cls_same, sess_same) {
  ix <- test_same == cls_same & same_session == sess_same
  k <- if (cls_same) sum(pred_same[ix]) else sum(!pred_same[ix])
  cp <- if (sum(ix) > 0) binom.test(k, sum(ix))$conf.int else c(NA, NA)
  data.frame(Pair_class = if (cls_same) "Same writer" else "Different writers",
             Sessions = if (sess_same) "Same session" else "Different sessions",
             n = sum(ix), Correct = k, Rate = if (sum(ix) > 0) k / sum(ix) else NA, CI_low = cp[1], CI_high = cp[2])
}
sess_tab <- rbind(cond(TRUE, TRUE), cond(TRUE, FALSE), cond(FALSE, TRUE), cond(FALSE, FALSE))
fisher_p <- function(cls_same) {
  a <- sess_tab[sess_tab$Pair_class == if (cls_same) "Same writer" else "Different writers", ]
  if (any(a$n == 0)) return(NA_real_)
  fisher.test(matrix(c(a$Correct[1], a$n[1] - a$Correct[1], a$Correct[2], a$n[2] - a$Correct[2]), 2))$p.value
}
p_same_writer_sessions <- fisher_p(TRUE); p_diff_writer_sessions <- fisher_p(FALSE)

# By anchor writer (writer of the first image in each test pair)
anchor <- meta$person_id[te_pairs[, 1]]
by_writer <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(anchor)), function(w) {
  ix <- anchor == w
  tmr <- mean(pred_same[ix & test_same]); tnr <- mean(!pred_same[ix & !test_same])
  data.frame(Writer = w, Pairs = sum(ix), Same_pairs = sum(ix & test_same),
             TMR = tmr, TNR = tnr, Bal_acc = (tmr + tnr) / 2, AUC = auc_dist(test_distance[ix], test_same[ix]))
}))

# By digit (the digit is the same in both images)
pair_digit <- meta$digit[te_pairs[, 1]]
by_digit <- do.call(rbind, lapply(0:4, function(dg) {
  ix <- which(pair_digit == dg)
  bs <- replicate(500, { i <- sample(ix, replace = TRUE); bal_acc(test_distance[i], test_same[i], threshold) })
  data.frame(Digit = dg, Pairs = length(ix), Bal_acc = bal_acc(test_distance[ix], test_same[ix], threshold),
             CI_low = unname(quantile(bs, .025)), CI_high = unname(quantile(bs, .975)))
}))
```

```{r}
                 set = rep(c("Training", "Validation"), each = length(history_siam$metrics$loss)),

  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Training = okabe[["blue"]], Validation = okabe[["red"]]), name = NULL) +
```

## What Task 3 tells us

On three writers the network never saw during training, the Siamese network separated same-writer from different-writer pairs well. At the distance threshold of 0.58 chosen on the validation pairs, balanced accuracy on the test pairs was 0.930 (95% bootstrap CI 0.917 to 0.941), with a true match rate of 0.931 and a true non-match rate of 0.929 (@tbl-t3-metrics, @tbl-t3-confusion). The AUC of 0.983 (95% CI 0.979 to 0.988) shows that the ranking of pairs by distance is good over all thresholds, not only at the one chosen (@fig-t3-roc, @fig-t3-dist; AUC is the probability that a random same-writer pair has a smaller distance than a random different-writer pair [@hanley1982; @fawcett2006]). Early stopping kept the weights from epoch 4 (validation loss 0.105) and stopped at epoch 6 (@fig-t3-loss). The test balanced accuracy is higher than the 0.877 seen on the validation pairs at the chosen threshold. With only three writers in each of the two sets, that difference could come from which writers happened to be in each set, so we do not read anything into it.

Task 1 predicted that pairs from different sessions would be harder, and the session breakdown shows this for same-writer pairs (@tbl-t3-session). All 200 same-writer pairs from the same session were accepted (100%, exact CI 98.2% to 100%), against 91.3% (689 of 755) for same-writer pairs from different sessions (Fisher exact p = `r fp(p_same_writer_sessions)`). For different-writer pairs there was no clear session effect (91.4% against 93.2%, p = `r fp(p_diff_writer_sessions)`). In other words, the network is least sure when asked to connect two sessions of one person, which is the case the application cares about. The same-session figure of 100% is also not independent evidence, since those images are near-copies.

Performance differed a little between the three test writers (balanced accuracy 0.960, 0.926 and 0.903 for writers 18, 19 and 20; @tbl-t3-writer), and between digits (@fig-t3-digit). With three writers and the pairs sharing images (2 000 test pairs use 2 475 distinct images, @tbl-t3-pairs), the intervals in @tbl-t3-metrics are likely to be too narrow, so they should be read as the lower bound on the uncertainty.

The CNN and the Siamese network answer different questions. The CNN has to pick one writer out of 20 (chance 5%) and was tested on the same writers in a new session, whereas the Siamese network makes a yes/no decision (chance 50%) on new writers. The two accuracy figures are therefore not directly comparable, and a fair comparison needs both models to be evaluated on the same footing, which we return to later in the report.
